designer_note: Feel-bearing networking values, kept out of code literals so that tuning 'does movement feel right' never means editing Rust or C#. What is deliberately NOT here: tick_hz (a world constant on the worlds row, I-19), the quantisation scales and integer ranges (ADR-0009), and the integrator identity and the ban on transcendental functions (ADR-0010). Those are laws, not tunables — a value in data that changes nothing when edited is worse than no value at all.

snapshot.note: 10 Hz is what the budget above produced, not a preference: 31 ships at 20 Hz measured ~289 KiB/s per session, over the 192 KiB/s budget. snapshot_interval_ticks = tick_hz / snapshot_hz = 2. If the budget is still exceeded, the next step is 5 Hz paired with remote_interp_delay_ms 400. Never buy bandwidth by lowering tick_hz — that rewrites the game-time meaning of every stored event (ADR-0006 §3).

input.note: One input per tick, so input rate stays at tick rate even though snapshots halved to 10 Hz — the client predicts every tick and only hears back every second tick. carry_forward_max_ticks 10 (500 ms) keeps one late packet from reading as a hiccup while stopping a disconnected ship from thrusting forever.

prediction.note: remote_interp_delay_ms is two snapshot intervals (2 x 100 ms), the same rule as before at 20 Hz — the number moved because the interval did. Cost: a remote ship is drawn 200 ms behind authority, which at 140 m/s is 28 m (about one greybox hull length). The ignore bands sit UNDER the four thresholds, not instead of them: the wire quantises position to 1 mm, so a perfectly correct client still disagrees by up to sqrt(3)/2 = 0.87 mm every snapshot, and without a band the correction machinery would run forever on that noise (ADR-0009 §2, ADR-0012).
